chapter: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
title: Charlie Parker plays the Kansas City Blues
summary: Parker asked to get a band together; she had him play, and he played a blues for the packed crowd with changes she had never heard.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: I said, "No, man, not the condition you're in." He said, "I'll do it, Mary. Anything you tell me I'll do." He said, "You know I'm not allowed to play in Birdland or any of the clubs." You know, that's during that period. So I told him, "Get up on the stand and let the people see how great you are." The place was really packed because see a lot of the people had followed me from the East Side. Some of these people had been to a ballet or something this night and they came in. They were all up in the balcony; it was Sunday night. Charlie Parker got up on the stand... he said, "Play the Kansas City Blues." Listen, I've never heard Coltrane play what that boy did! No! I talk about it often. When he finished the people in the place stood up and applauded. During the time that he played I don't know what carried us along with him because there were sounds that we'd never played before, Oscar and the bass and piano. To start out a blues - I think one of the guys had played one chorus...Charlie Parker kept going to keys and he kept going through changes... The one on the bass said, "Mary, where is he now?" I said, "Man, don't talk to me now," because Oscar said if anybody came up on the stand they were going to help him, so when Charlie stepped up there he said, "Lou, let's blow." So we were listening to his changes during it. I've never heard him play like that before in my life, the way he played.
When he finished everybody just screamed. He said, "How was that?" I said, "Man, that was too great for me."
But you still didn't go with him, in the band?
I didn't see him any more after that because later on I went to Europe. This was in the year of '52.
